div: The AI Assistant needs to know which large-language-model (LLM) service to talk to, how to authenticate with it, and which model to use. These settings are made in the "LLM Provider Settings" window. Until a provider is set up, the assistant shows a Configure LLM Provider button that opens this window; afterwards it is available from the menu in the upper-right corner of the assistant ("Configure LLM Provider…").

A provider is an API endpoint plus its API key; each provider has one or more models. You can set up several providers, and several models per provider, and mark the one to use as Active. When you press Accept, the settings are saved to a file named llm_config.xml in InterSpec's user data directory (see Help > About InterSpec > Data for its location).

ol.li: Choose your provider from the "Known providers…" drop-down to the right of the API endpoint field; this fills in the endpoint (and a suggested model).
Paste your API key into the Bearer token field.

Optionally press Fetch models to get the list of models your key can use, and pick one. When you pick or type a model name InterSpec knows about, its settings (image support, token limits, reasoning) are filled in for you.

div.p: The endpoint is the full URL that chat requests are sent to, including the path - not just the server name. For example, for OpenAI it is https://api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions, not just api.openai.com. The path also tells InterSpec which wire format (protocol) to use:

tr.td: OpenAI, and nearly every "OpenAI-compatible" service (Google Gemini, OpenRouter, xAI, Ask Sage, local servers, ...)
OpenAI's newer API; only needed for some of OpenAI's newest models

div.p: The detected format is shown next to the endpoint; if detection gets it wrong (e.g., a proxy with an unusual path), use the Override drop-down.
The endpoints of some well-known providers are:

tr.td: Not needed, unless the server was started with one

ul.li: OpenAI: some of the newest models (for example gpt-6-astra and gpt-6.1-sol) can only use tools - which the assistant relies on - through the Responses endpoint (/v1/responses).
Anthropic: use the native /v1/messages endpoint above, rather than Anthropic's OpenAI-compatible endpoint, which ignores the reasoning setting.
OpenRouter gives access to models from many vendors with one key; its model names include the vendor, e.g. anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5.

Ask Sage uses its own model names (e.g. google-gemini-2.5-pro), so use Fetch models to see the available ones. Use the host for your Ask Sage instance; your organization can tell you which that is. Ask Sage does not allow requests from web browsers, so check CORS fix if it is shown.

Local servers (Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM, llama.cpp, ...): start the server, and use its OpenAI-compatible endpoint, with the address and port the server reports when it starts. Local servers usually do not need an API key, so any text (or none) can be used for the token. Make sure the server's context size (e.g., Ollama's num_ctx) is at least as large as the Context limit you enter here. Small local models may struggle with the assistant's many tools; models with at least tens of billions of parameters, and good tool-calling support, work best.

div.p: Create an API key in your provider's web console (see the table above), and paste it into the Bearer token field. For most providers it is sent as an Authorization: Bearer header; for Anthropic's own API it is sent as the x-api-key header. The key is stored, unencrypted, in llm_config.xml in your user data directory. Use of most hosted providers is billed per token, so keep your key private.

Fetch models asks the provider for the list of models your key can use (from the endpoint's /models URL), so you can pick one rather than typing its name. Some providers (for example, OpenRouter) also report each model's context length, maximum output, and image support, which InterSpec then uses when you pick that model. Since these are the model's technical maximums, which can be far larger than is useful (or than your account allows to be requested), the suggested max tokens is limited to 64,000, and the context limit to 200,000; you can enter larger values yourself.

CORS fix (only in some builds): requests normally go out through the web browser engine InterSpec uses for its display, which some providers (for example, Ask Sage) refuse to answer because of their cross-origin (CORS) policy. Checking this sends that provider's requests from InterSpec itself instead.

Banner text (optional): a short note shown above the assistant's input field while that provider is active - for example, your organization's rules for what may be sent to it. It is saved as the <Banner> element of the provider in llm_config.xml. Leave it blank for no banner.

When you pick, or type, a model name that InterSpec knows about, the settings below are filled in with reasonable values; a note under the model name says when this happened. You can change them afterwards. The known models are listed in llm_model_presets.xml in InterSpec's data directory; to add or change entries, copy that file to your user data directory and edit it.

For a model InterSpec does not know, a note says so, and the settings are left as they are - check your provider's documentation for them ("Fetch models" can fill some in). A warning is shown under the model when a setting is known not to work with it - for example, reasoning turned on for a model without reasoning, a max tokens or context limit above what the provider reports, or an OpenAI model that needs the newer Responses endpoint. These warnings do not stop you from saving.

ul.li: Model name: the provider's identifier for the model, e.g. gpt-5-mini, claude-sonnet-5-5, or gemini-3.8-flash.

Max tokens: the maximum length of each response, in tokens (a token is roughly three-quarters of a word). Blank uses the provider's default; required for Anthropic. For reasoning models this limit includes the reasoning, so do not set it too low.

Context limit: the size of the model's context window, in tokens. When a conversation reaches about 85% of this, older parts of it are summarized to make room. This can be set below the model's true limit to keep long conversations from becoming slow and expensive. Blank means the conversation is never summarized.

Temperature: 0.0 to 2.0; lower values give more consistent answers. 0.2 - 0.5 is a good range; blank uses the provider's default. Not all models accept it (many reasoning models do not). It is not sent to Anthropic models while thinking is enabled, nor to the Claude models that do not accept it at all (Opus 4.7 and later, Sonnet and Haiku 5 and later, and Fable).
Supports images: check if the model accepts images; the assistant can then look at pictures of the spectrum, and you can attach photos to your questions.
Force tool use: forces the model to call a tool at steps of a workflow where one is expected. Helps some models (often open-weight ones) that stop calling tools part-way through a task.

Reasoning: whether, and how hard, the model "thinks" before answering. Off sends nothing. Low, Medium, and High set the reasoning effort; more effort is slower and uses more tokens, but usually gives better analysis. On turns reasoning on without an effort level (for OpenRouter-style APIs). For the OpenAI Chat format the effort is sent as reasoning_effort; for the OpenAI Responses format as reasoning.effort; for Anthropic, any setting other than Off turns on Claude's thinking - for Claude 4.6 and later the effort is sent as output_config.effort (with On using the model's default effort), and for older models it sets the thinking budget. Only use this for models that support reasoning, or the provider may reject the request.
Instructions: how detailed the instructions InterSpec gives the model are. Verbose can help smaller models; Terse is enough for the most capable ones.

MCP server (desktop versions): lets other AI applications use InterSpec's tools via the Model Context Protocol, at http://127.0.0.1:<port>/mcp-api. Set a bearer token that clients must supply. You can separately allow clients to submit prompts to the assistant, and to directly run the assistant's specialized agents; both of those require an LLM provider to be configured.

Network (some builds): a proxy URL, an extra certificate bundle to trust (for networks that inspect HTTPS traffic), and, as a last resort, turning off certificate checks. These only apply to providers using the CORS fix.
Conversation logs: saves each conversation as an XML file in the llm_logs folder of the user data directory.

div.p: The saved llm_config.xml contains comments describing each setting. You can share it, or drag it onto InterSpec (on another computer, say) to import it; you will be asked before an existing configuration is replaced. Hand-made comments are not kept when the settings window saves the file again. A few advanced settings can only be set by editing the file:

ul.li: <KnowledgeBaseRagUrl>, <KnowledgeBaseRagModel>, <KnowledgeBaseRagCorpora>: an optional retrieval-augmented-generation service for the KnowledgeBase sub-agent to search. This is a separate service that is not distributed with InterSpec, so these should normally be left out.
<CompactionSystemPrompt>: replaces the instructions used when summarizing older parts of a long conversation.
<DebugFile>: stdout, stderr, or a file path, to write detailed debugging information about the assistant's requests and tool calls.

<HttpBackend> (and the httpBackend attribute of an <ApiProvider>): auto (the default: use the provider's setting, otherwise the browser), browser, or native, to choose how requests are sent (the CORS fix sets this per provider).

div.p: When you use the assistant, your questions, information about the loaded spectra and analysis results, and (for models that support images) pictures of the spectrum are sent to the provider you configure. Follow your organization's rules about which providers may be used for your data; a locally running model keeps everything on your computer.
